questions.q: In this lesson's worked trace, why does the question 'Which table has customer churn data?' need to be embedded with the same model used for the indexed chunks?
options: Because vectors from different embedding models aren't comparable, and similarity search depends on comparing the question's vector against the chunk vectors
Because the question doesn't actually need to be embedded at all
Because Fabric requires all queries to use KQL syntax instead of embeddings
Because embedding models change automatically between index time and query time
questions.explain: This is the same rule from Lesson 51: every chunk and every question must use the same embedding model, or the vectors can't be meaningfully compared.

questions.q: Why did retrieval return the DimCustomer chunk for the churn question in this worked example?
options: Because 'churn' appeared in both the table's description and its churn_risk_score column, matching closely with the embedded question
Because DimCustomer was the only table in the entire catalog
Because the pipeline was hardcoded to always return DimCustomer
Because DimCustomer was alphabetically first in the index
questions.explain: Retrieval finds the stored vector closest in meaning to the question's vector — here, the churn-related content in DimCustomer's chunk matched best.

questions.q: Why does the generated answer explicitly name its source table and workspace?
options: Because that's the direct payoff of storing metadata alongside each vector — it lets the answer be traced back and verified rather than being an unverifiable claim
Because naming a source table is required by KQL syntax
Because it makes the answer sound more confident regardless of accuracy
Because without a name, the LLM cannot generate any response at all
questions.explain: Lesson 51 established that index metadata (table, workspace) is what enables this traceability — this lesson shows the payoff in the final answer.

questions.q: What is the key distinction this lesson draws between 'grounding' and 'verification'?
options: Grounding in retrieved content prevents hallucination, but it doesn't guarantee the retrieved source itself was accurate — a stale catalog entry gets confidently repeated
Grounding and verification mean exactly the same thing
Verification is unnecessary once a RAG pipeline is in place
Grounding only applies to PySpark code, never to RAG answers
questions.explain: If the DimCustomer catalog entry were itself stale or wrong, the RAG pipeline would confidently retrieve and repeat that staleness — grounding fixes hallucination, not bad source data.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect to the chapter's earlier review habit from Lessons 45, 46, and 48?
options: It applies the same 'generated output still needs to be checked against something real' discipline, now to a RAG-grounded answer citing its source
It abandons that review habit since RAG is assumed to always be correct
It has no connection to the earlier lessons in this chapter
It only applies to KQL queries, not to RAG pipelines
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly closes this loop: a grounded answer is more reliable than an ungrounded guess, but 'more reliable' still isn't the same as 'verified.'
